title: Nvidia Investigates CEO's Affair with Alleged Chinese Spy
paragraphs: US chipmaker Nvidia has launched an investigation into reports that its CEO, Jensen Huang, was targeted by Chinese intelligence after he admitted having an affair with a businesswoman suspected of spying for Beijing.
The company's board announced the investigation on November 8, following reports by The New York Times that US intelligence officials believed the woman was gathering information for China.
In a letter to employees, Huang, 63, admitted being unfaithful to his wife and apologized to his family and colleagues. He said he took "full responsibility" for his actions.
Nvidia's board said it had "no reason to believe" that national security or company secrets had been compromised, but that it would examine all available information.
Huang has promised to cooperate fully and will remain CEO during the investigation.
"I love our country and our company," he wrote. "I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security."

Nvidia has become a major player in the global race to develop artificial intelligence (AI), with its advanced computer chips powering many AI systems. These chips have also been subject to US export restrictions aimed at limiting China's access to advanced technology.

The New York Times identified the woman as Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and chip buyer. She previously worked as a television reporter in China before becoming a top executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years.
The company previously faced accusations of helping businesses sidestep US export restrictions. However, Nvidia said its own checks found no illegal activity.
The scandal has also led to legal action. On November 9, a shareholder sued Nvidia and Huang, accusing them of misleading investors about the affair and its possible risks to the business.
Nvidia shares fell 4.3% that day, wiping about $190 billion off its market value. They dropped another 5.5% on November 10.
Meanwhile, President Donald Trump said the FBI was also looking into the affair, but added that Huang had told him he had no idea the woman could be involved in espionage.
China has rejected the spying allegations, calling them unsubstantiated.
